Learning algorithms

Meeting 3. Memory, similarity, and search

Course meeting 23

A fitted neural network stores learned weights and biases. It can use those numbers to predict without consulting its training rows again. Another kind of predictor keeps the examples themselves. When a new observation arrives, it retrieves relevant examples and uses their answers. The central questions are then what counts as relevant, how the retrieved evidence becomes a prediction, and how much work it takes to find it.

A fragment of a song and a query word make these questions concrete. A noisy recording can identify a stored song even though the recorded waveforms are not identical. A word vector can retrieve nearby words without asking for a particular word's identifier. Both systems consult stored information, but their representations and matching rules differ.

The main points

  1. An observation can be a query.

    Choose a representation and a rule for comparing it with stored examples. Exact lookup of small fingerprints can support recognition of an imperfect recording.

  2. Neighbors can supply an answer.

    Nearby labeled examples can vote for a class or contribute to a numerical prediction. The number of neighbors and their weights affect the result.

  3. Retaining examples is a form of learning.

    Ordinary nearest-neighbor prediction uses a memory that grows with the training set. Fitting can still involve preprocessing and an expensive index build.

  4. Organizing memory costs work before it saves work.

    A balanced tree can be built by median partitions. Its construction cost depends on how the medians are found.

  5. A partition boundary does not stop similarity.

    The closest point may lie across a split. Exact search needs backtracking and valid distance bounds.

  6. Count coordinates, points, regions, and queries separately.

    A short tree can still require a long search. The value of an index depends on geometry and how often it is reused.

  7. Approximation needs an accuracy measurement.

    A smaller search budget or a smaller representation can change the neighbors. Measure both retrieval quality and any resulting prediction error.

1. Asking a memory about an observation

A familiar database query supplies a known key: return the row whose song identifier is a particular value. Now imagine hearing music in a busy restaurant. You have a short recording mixed with voices and other noise. You do not have the song's identifier; finding that identifier is the task. A query is the information supplied to a search. Here the query is an observation rather than a known name.

There is a similar distinction for words. A catalog may contain a vector for each word. Asking for the vector stored under piano is a lookup by name. Asking which other vectors are close to it is a similarity search. Database systems can support many kinds of queries, including similarity queries; the distinction is between these two questions, not a limitation of all databases.

A representation is the information we keep from an observation for a task. It might be a vector of numerical features or a collection of compact tokens. Retrieval means finding stored items that satisfy a matching or relevance rule. The rule becomes precise only after we choose the representation and comparison.

Shazam: imperfect observations, exact token lookups

In the classic Shazam method, distinctive time-frequency landmarks become compact fingerprint tokens. A query token can be looked up exactly in an index of stored token occurrences. Many matches supporting one recording at a common time offset provide evidence for identification. Some tokens can be lost to noise while enough others still agree. Thus exact matching of tokens does not require identity of the raw recordings. This describes the classic fingerprinting method, not a claim about every component of the current service. [1]

A query fragment also starts partway through a longer recording. If several matched tokens have reference time minus query time close to the same offset, they point to one plausible alignment. A single token hit may be accidental; agreement across tokens matters. A separate family of neural audio-retrieval systems learns audio vectors and searches those vectors. Such systems connect naturally to word embeddings, but they should not be confused with classic Shazam's fingerprint index. [2]

Word embeddings: what does nearby mean?

A word embedding represents a word by a vector learned from patterns of word use. The course catalog contains 50,000 GloVe word vectors. Its coordinates let us compute a numerical similarity; whether that similarity is useful depends on the task. Words occurring in related contexts may be nearby even if they are not synonyms. [3]

The scores below use cosine similarity, a comparison of vector directions ranging from -1 to 1. Larger scores mean more closely aligned directions. The next section develops the calculation.

2. Turning similarity into a calculation

Let x be a vector of input features and q a query represented in the same coordinates. We will use the following notation. A target is an observed answer attached to a training example: a class label or a numerical value.

Notation used throughout the notes
SymbolMeaning
nNumber of stored examples
dCoordinates per example
kNumber of neighbors requested, from 1 to n
QNumber of queries processed
xᵢ, yᵢInput vector and observed target for stored example i
q, ŷ(q)A query and the prediction made for it

Euclidean distance measures straight-line separation in the chosen coordinates. It combines the coordinate differences by squaring them, summing them, and taking a square root.

dist(q,x)=∑j=1d(qj−xj)2.

In words: The Euclidean distance from query q to stored vector x is the square root of the sum, over the d coordinates, of the squared difference between q and x in each coordinate.

Cosine similarity compares directions. The norm of a vector is its Euclidean length. For nonzero vectors, divide each vector by its norm, then take their dot product. A dot product multiplies corresponding coordinates and sums the products.

cos(u,v)=u·v‖u‖‖v‖=(u‖u‖)·(v‖v‖).

In words: Cosine similarity of nonzero vectors u and v is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. Equivalently, it is the dot product of their unit-length normalized vectors.

Aligned directions have cosine 1; perpendicular directions have cosine 0; opposite directions have cosine -1. Cosine 1 does not require identical original vectors: one can be a positive multiple of the other. Most pairs of distinct vectors are not perpendicular. A negative cosine is a geometric statement, not a general rule that two words are antonyms.

For unit vectors, the two comparisons give the same ranking: larger cosine means smaller Euclidean distance. Expand the square of their difference to see why.

‖u−v‖2=u·u+v·v−2u·v=2−2(u·v).

In words: For unit vectors u and v, their squared Euclidean distance equals u dot u plus v dot v minus twice u dot v, which is two minus twice their dot product.

Units are part of the representation

Changing the currency used to report an amount can greatly change its numerical size without changing what the amount represents. Similarly, dollars and cents differ by a factor of 100. A distance calculation on unscaled features sees those numerical changes. If one feature is measured in years and another in dollars, the larger numerical scale can dominate the result.

Feature standardization subtracts a feature's training mean and divides by its training standard deviation. It scales columns of the data table. This is a different operation from normalizing each row vector to length one for cosine comparison. Neither operation is automatically appropriate for every task; the chosen geometry should make useful examples close.

Changing the nearest example by changing the scale

In the six-point example, the query is (1.5, 110). The raw-coordinate nearest example is C = (4, 105), at distance about 5.59. After standardizing both coordinates with the training means and scales, the nearest example is A = (1, 100). The stored observations did not change; the comparison did. Explore the six-point example in the slides.

Fit any learned preprocessing statistics on training data. Transform validation observations and future queries with those same saved statistics. Fitting a new scaler separately to a query would put it in a different coordinate system from the stored examples.

3. From retrieved neighbors to a prediction

Suppose each stored input has an observed target. A new query has known inputs but an unknown target. A k-nearest-neighbor predictor, abbreviated kNN, finds the k closest stored training inputs and combines their targets. Retrieval chooses the evidence; the prediction rule decides how to use it.

Classification: a vote and a vote fraction

For classification, targets are class labels. If the eleven nearest examples include nine red labels and two blue labels, uniform voting predicts red. The red vote fraction is 9/11, approximately 0.818. That fraction supplies a local class-probability estimate, but it is not a guarantee that the prediction has an 81.8% chance of being correct. The representation, neighborhood, sampling, and calibration all matter.

A piece of music may remind a listener of more than one style. Resemblance provides evidence rather than an automatic identification. The analogous statistical question is whether nearby labeled examples are informative about a new target. Physical proximity alone need not be useful: two people sitting next to each other need not have similar ages. The feature representation must support the prediction task.

Regression: average the neighboring targets

For regression, the target is a number. Uniform kNN regression averages the targets of the retrieved examples. Write Nk(q) for the set of indices of the k nearest training inputs to q.

y^(q)=1k∑i∈Nk(q)yi.

In words: The uniform k-nearest-neighbor prediction for query q is one divided by k times the sum of the observed targets of the k training inputs nearest to q.

For example, if five relevant comparison cases have ages 19, 20, 20, 21, and 22, their mean is 20.4. The arithmetic averages the targets; it does not average the input coordinates and call that the target.

The regression experiment below has noisy observations of a smooth generating function. The dashed curve shows that function because this is a synthetic experiment. A predictor is given the training inputs and noisy targets, not the hidden generating curve. The solid prediction curve is obtained by moving the query along the input axis and repeatedly applying the same neighbor rule.

The controls also report mean squared error (MSE), the average squared difference between a prediction and its observed target. Training MSE uses the stored training examples; validation MSE uses separate observations held out from fitting. Smaller MSE means better agreement on the evaluated examples.

With one neighbor, the prediction can jump whenever a different training point becomes closest. An unusually high noisy observation can pull up predictions throughout the region where it is nearest. With many neighbors, averaging reduces sensitivity to individual targets, but can wash out a real pattern. Small k can overfit; large k can underfit. A smoother-looking curve is not itself evidence of better prediction.

4. What fitting retains, and what validation chooses

The familiar interface still applies: choose a model, fit it on training inputs and targets, and predict for other inputs. In ordinary kNN, fitting retains access to the training examples and their targets. It may also fit preprocessing and build a search index, a data structure that organizes examples so queries can skip unnecessary comparisons. An index does not eliminate the coordinates or targets needed to answer the query.

Ordinary kNN is called non-parametric because its retained predictive state can grow with the number of training examples instead of being restricted to a fixed-size vector of learned coefficients. This does not mean there are no numbers or choices. The neighbor count, metric, weights, and preprocessing are still settings. In contrast, a neural network with a fixed architecture has a fixed number of weights and biases even when it is trained on more rows. A learned neural representation followed by kNN combines the two ideas.

A hyperparameter is a setting chosen for the learning procedure rather than a coefficient learned by its fitting updates. The neighbor count k is a hyperparameter. Use validation examples to compare choices under a stated evaluation metric. Classification accuracy is the fraction of labels predicted correctly. For regression, mean squared error (MSE) averages the squared differences between predictions and observed targets; smaller is better.

Validation selects k = 3 for this classification split and k = 5 for this regression split. Neither number is universally best. The six candidates are compared on the same split within each experiment. Test observations remain reserved for a final assessment of the selected procedure.

Why one neighbor can get zero training error

If every training input location is distinct and a query may retrieve itself, its closest training input is itself at distance zero. A one-neighbor predictor therefore returns its own stored target. This explains perfect training predictions without establishing useful predictions on new inputs. Duplicate inputs with conflicting targets require a tie rule and cannot all be fitted exactly by one deterministic prediction at that location.

Leaving a query out of its candidate set changes this calculation. A nearest-word demonstration excludes the query word to avoid the trivial answer. Validation evaluates observations held out from fitting. A reported training score must say whether the training rows can retrieve themselves.

A classifier with training-only standardization

Assume the training and validation arrays have already been separated. Each row of X_train is an input and each entry of y_train is its class label. A pipeline applies the same saved transformation before every prediction.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3, weights="uniform"),
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_valid)
validation_accuracy = (predictions == y_valid).mean()

The call to predict does not add validation rows to the training memory. predict_proba can return class vote fractions. Libraries may choose a full scan or an index according to their settings and data. [4]

5. The full scan is the baseline

Suppose you have a million vectors and want the closest five to a query. One dependable method is to compare the query with every vector, then select the best five. This full scan, also called exhaustive search, gives a baseline for both correctness and cost.

For normalized word vectors, put the stored row vectors in a matrix U with n rows and d columns. Treat the query q as a row vector, so its transpose is a column vector. One matrix-vector multiplication produces all cosine scores.

U∈Rn×d,q∈R1×d,s=UqT∈Rn×1.

In words: U has n rows and d columns. Query q has one row and d columns. Multiplying U by the transpose of q produces an n-by-one column of dot-product similarity scores.

Writing this as one operation in code does not make its arithmetic constant. Each of the n rows contributes d coordinate products. Efficient numerical libraries can make the computation fast through batching, vectorization, and hardware parallelism while still performing work proportional to nd.

We use O(f) for an asymptotic upper bound proportional to f, and Θ(f) when that order describes both upper and lower growth, under the stated computation model. A dense d-coordinate distance or dot product takes Θ(d) arithmetic work. Computing one for every stored vector takes Θ(nd).

Selecting the best k is a separate operation. It does not require fully sorting all n scores. A linear-time selection algorithm can isolate the best k, after which sorting just those winners takes O(k log k). The combined bound is O(nd + n + k log k). A max-heap is a data structure that keeps the largest value available at its root while supporting efficient updates. For nearest neighbors, that value is the farthest retained candidate's distance. A streaming implementation can maintain a heap of k candidates, adding O(n log k) candidate-management work for k at least two; for one neighbor, each update is constant work.

6. Organizing space with a kd-tree

Binary search narrows a search in a sorted array by repeatedly ruling out half the entries. To organize vectors, we can also divide a collection in halves, but now the divisions concern coordinates in space. A kd-tree is a binary spatial tree: each internal node splits its region along one coordinate, and its two children represent the two resulting parts.

In the two-coordinate example, start with sixteen points. Split the first coordinate near its median, leaving eight points on each side. Within each half, split the second coordinate near its own median. Continue alternating coordinates. In d dimensions, cycle through the d coordinates; each split still has two children.

The name kd-tree historically refers to the number of coordinate dimensions. Here we use d for dimension and reserve k for the number of neighbors requested. The same tree supports different values of query k. Its partitions do not have to be rebuilt when we request three neighbors instead of one.

  1. Choose the split coordinate, cycling with depth.
  2. Select the middle value and partition the point references into two balanced groups. Apply a consistent tie rule when coordinates are equal.
  3. Record the split and recursively build the two children.
  4. Stop at a small leaf bucket, which retains its examples.

The median balances the number of points, not necessarily the geometric widths of the regions. An internal node records a split coordinate and threshold, and a leaf stores a small bucket of examples or references to them. The region of each node contains every point below it. That containment is the fact exact search will use.

Why construction can cost O(n log n)

To see the cost, count work by levels. At the root, all n points participate. At the next level, the two groups have about n/2 points each. At the following level, four groups have about n/4 each. At every level, the total number of points across groups is still n.

Assume the coordinate is chosen cyclically, a coordinate access costs constant time, and a split moves point references rather than copying whole vectors. A linear-time median-selection algorithm followed by partitioning takes O(m) work on a group of size m. Therefore a whole level costs O(n). Balanced groups give O(log n) split levels, so the partitioning cost is O(n log n). Constant leaf-bucket size does not change that asymptotic bound.

T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n)=O(nlogn).

In words: For balanced median partitioning with linear work at a node, the build recurrence is T of n equals twice T of about n over two plus O of n. Its solution is O of n log n.

If each recursive subset is fully sorted instead, the level costs are O(n log n), O(n log(n/2)), and so on. Their sum is O(n log² n) for fixed dimension. That is the cost of the simple recursive-sort construction in the companion notebook. The interactive construction uses linear-time median selection. Presorting by all d coordinates and maintaining those orders is another construction strategy, commonly analyzed as O(dn log n); these are different algorithms, not interchangeable bounds. [5]

Dimension has not disappeared from storage. The input coordinates occupy Θ(nd) numbers and must be read or retained. A compact cyclic-split tree can add O(n) nodes and references; storing an explicit d-coordinate bounding box at every node adds up to O(nd) metadata in a straightforward implementation. Always say whether a space bound counts the examples, the index overhead, or both.

Keep the costs separate

Reading or copying dense coordinates costs Θ(nd). Cyclic median partitioning with linear selection adds O(n log n). Computing training means and scales and transforming all rows costs O(nd); applying those saved statistics to one query costs O(d). If full bounding boxes are stored at every node, initializing them adds O(nd) work and storage. An end-to-end build bound must include the operations the implementation actually performs.

7. Exact search needs more than one descent

An exact nearest-neighbor search returns the true closest stored points under the specified representation, distance, and tie convention. Exact here refers to the correctness of the neighbor result. It does not mean the query must be identical to a stored row.

Start by following the split containing the query, down to a leaf, and compute distances to its points. The best candidate so far is the incumbent: an answer that another point might improve. This first leaf need not contain the true nearest point. A query can lie just to the left of a split while its closest point lies just to the right.

The boundary-crossing query

The root split is x₁ = 6 and the query is q = (5.95, 4.3). It descends on the left. Point G = (5.4, 4.2) has distance about 0.559. But point I = (6.2, 4.3), across the split, has distance 0.25. Stopping at the first leaf would miss I. The query is only 0.05 from the right-hand region, so that region cannot yet be ruled out.

Backtracking means returning to an earlier node to consider another branch. Pruning means skipping an entire region because a valid bound shows it cannot improve the current candidates. The algorithm does not first inspect every point in a pruned region; the region's geometry supplies the bound.

For a rectangular region, let aj and bj be the lower and upper limits in coordinate j. The query's coordinate gap is zero when it lies inside that interval, and otherwise is its distance to the closer endpoint. Combining these gaps gives a lower bound on the distance to every point in the region.

δj=max(aj−qj,0,qj−bj),L(q,region)=∑j=1dδj2.

In words: For each coordinate j, the gap delta j is the maximum of a j minus q j, zero, and q j minus b j. The distance lower bound for the region is the square root of the sum of these squared coordinate gaps.

For one neighbor, the current search radius is the incumbent's distance. For k neighbors, keep the best k candidates found so far and use the farthest of those candidates as the radius. Until k candidates have been found, treat the radius as infinite. If the region's lower bound exceeds the current radius, every point there is too far to help.

L(q,region)>ρ⟹prune the region.

In words: Prune a region when its distance lower bound L is strictly greater than rho, the distance of the farthest retained candidate. Before k candidates exist, rho is infinite.

Strict inequality is a conservative choice when equal-distance ties must be handled consistently. The traversal visits the nearer child first to find useful candidates early, then tests whether the farther child could improve them. As better candidates arrive, the radius shrinks and more regions may be pruned.

8. What does a query actually cost?

For the boundary-crossing example with k = 1, the tree checks four point distances, to D, G, I, and J, rather than all sixteen. It also computes eleven region bounds, traverses nodes, compares values, and updates candidates. Four point-distance calls are not four total operations. In d dimensions, both a dense point distance and a full rectangular-region bound require Θ(d) coordinate work.

Let m be the number of points whose distances are computed and V the number of regions whose bounds are tested. With a max-heap, the farthest retained candidate is available at the heap's root, and a candidate update takes O(log k) work for k at least two. Sorting the final answers, if requested, adds O(k log k).

O(dV+dm+mlogk+klogk).

In words: With full rectangular bounds and a max-heap, a useful bound is O of d times V plus d times m plus m log k plus k log k: region bounds, point distances, candidate updates, and sorting the returned neighbors. The heap update cost is constant when k is one.

The interactive demonstration keeps its tiny candidate list sorted for clarity. The displayed bound describes the max-heap implementation; sorting the whole candidate list after every update would add more work when k grows.

A balanced tree has logarithmic height, but the query can visit several branches. In the worst case, V and m can both be proportional to n. For fixed k, exact search can therefore take O(nd) work under this model. Its point-distance work alone can match a full scan. For varying k, keep the candidate-management and output terms rather than silently treating them as constants.

Binary search on a sorted list can rule out one half from the ordering. A nearest-neighbor query needs geometric evidence before it can rule out the other half. That is why the height of the tree does not by itself bound all the work. Bounds for reporting points inside a fixed rectangular range answer a different query and should not be substituted for nearest-neighbor complexity.

Pay once to save on many queries

Separate index construction from query processing. Let B be the build cost, s the cost of one full scan, and t the cost of one indexed query. If these per-query costs remain roughly stable, the total costs for Q queries are:

Cscan=Qs,Ctree=B+Qt,Q>Bs−t when s>t.

In words: The total full-scan cost is Q times s. The total indexed cost is B plus Q times t. If s is greater than t, indexing becomes cheaper when Q is greater than B divided by s minus t.

If t is at least s and building has a positive cost, this simple model has no break-even point. Repeating a slower indexed query will not repay the build. If the representation or catalog changes and the index must be rebuilt, include that cost too.

9. Dimension affects arithmetic and pruning

More coordinates have an immediate arithmetic and storage cost. The 50,000-word catalog illustrates this without any asymptotic notation: 300 coordinates is six times 50 coordinates. A float32 coordinate occupies four bytes; the table counts vector coordinates only, using decimal megabytes.

Coordinate costs for 50,000 stored word vectors
Coordinates dfloat32 storageCoordinate products in one normalized-dot-product full scan
5010 MB2.5 million
30060 MB15 million

There is also a geometric effect. In some high-dimensional datasets, the region bounds fail to exclude much of the data. The tree then checks nearly every point and also pays for its traversal and bounds. A well-implemented full scan may be faster.

The timing entries are medians of five runs on one machine. The query columns measure the entire batch of 100 queries, while the build column is separate. Exact neighbor distances were checked against the exhaustive result. At 50 and 300 dimensions, this tree computes all 300,000 point distances and is slower than the full scan. These are measurements of this experiment, not universal dimension thresholds.

The distribution of points, effective or intrinsic dimension of their variation, metric, bucket size, k, query batch, and implementation all affect performance. A larger k can make the candidate radius larger and reduce pruning. A two-dimensional picture of an embedding is useful for illustration, but it does not establish which points are nearest in the original high-dimensional representation.

10. Spending less work and measuring the loss

An approximate neighbor search is allowed to return something other than the exact top k. Two distinct approaches are to examine fewer candidates in the same representation, or to search in a smaller representation. They can save different kinds of work and need separate accuracy checks.

A limit on point-distance calculations

One simple approximation stops a depth-first tree search after a point-distance budget is exhausted. The earlier bounds remain valid, but an unvisited region may still contain a closer point when the budget runs out. Recall@k is the fraction of the exact top-k items recovered by the approximate result, using a consistent tie convention.

recall@k=|Nkapprox(q)∩Nkexact(q)|k.

In words: Recall at k equals the number of items shared by the approximate and exact top-k sets, divided by k.

The experiment uses the same sixteen stored points and k = 3. For the boundary-crossing query, the exact neighbors are I, G, and E. A four-distance budget returns G, D, and B, recovering one of the three. The validation table aggregates 48 other query locations. For this toy regression task, the target at a point is sin(0.6x₁) + 0.15x₂, and a prediction averages the three retrieved targets.

Actual retrieval and prediction measurements on 48 separate validation queries
BudgetMean recall@3Mean point distancesPrediction MSE

Exact retrieval guarantees the correct neighbors for the chosen distance. It does not guarantee a perfect statistical predictor. In this particular toy experiment, an approximate result can even have slightly lower prediction MSE while having worse neighbor recall. Measure retrieval fidelity and downstream prediction quality separately; a favorable result on one validation set is not a general guarantee.

Reduce the coordinates with one shared map

A random projection multiplies the input vectors by a suitably sampled random matrix to obtain fewer coordinates. Let the original matrix U have shape n by d. Choose a projection matrix R of shape d by r, where r is the reduced dimension and is separate from the neighbor count k.

U⏟n×dR⏟d×r=Z⏟n×r,q⏟1×dR⏟d×r=z⏟1×r.

In words: Multiplying the n-by-d data matrix U by the d-by-r projection matrix R gives the n-by-r matrix Z. A one-by-d query row q is multiplied by the same R to obtain a one-by-r query row z.

The shape example of 1,000 vectors with 500 coordinates becoming 1,000 vectors with 10 coordinates illustrates the potential savings. It does not establish that ten coordinates preserve the desired neighbors. Results such as the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma give probabilistic distance-distortion guarantees for finite collections when the reduced dimension is large enough for the requested distortion and confidence. The parameters of that guarantee matter. [6]

Even a small distance distortion can reverse nearly tied neighbors. If two original distances are 1.00 and 1.01, allowing each to change by a few percent leaves room for their order to swap. Preserving approximate distances is therefore weaker than preserving the exact ordered top k.

Actual neighbors before and after projection; smaller distances rank first
RankOriginal 300-DDistanceProjectedDistanceRecovered?

This comparison uses the offline vocabulary of 125 GloVe words: each query has 124 candidates after excluding itself. It is a smaller catalog than the 50,000-word example above. The original 300-dimensional vectors are normalized first; the shared Gaussian projection is then applied, and the projected vectors are not renormalized. Original unit-vector Euclidean rankings agree with cosine rankings. Recall measures recovery of the original five neighbors. Changing the dimension or random seed need not improve each individual query monotonically.

If original vectors are retained to recheck retrieved candidates, their storage also remains. Projection can reduce future query work, but its initial multiplication and any index rebuild still belong in the cost calculation.

11. Four close neighbors and one farther away

Uniform averaging gives every selected target weight 1/k. Suppose the five nearest neighbors include four close to the query and a fifth much farther away. They are all among the nearest five, but distance gives a reason to consider unequal influence. One choice is inverse-distance weighting: assign a larger raw weight to a smaller positive distance, then normalize the weights so they sum to one.

Let δi be the distance to retrieved neighbor i, and wi its normalized contribution weight. The sum below is over the selected neighbors.

wi=1/δi∑j1/δj,∑iwi=1,y^=∑iwiyi.

In words: For positive neighbor distances delta i, weight w i is one over delta i divided by the sum of one over delta j across selected neighbors. The weights sum to one, and the prediction is the sum of each weight times its neighbor's target.

Three targets: work out the normalized weights

Take distances 0.2, 0.4, and 0.8, with targets 3, 5, and 8. Uniform averaging gives (3 + 5 + 8)/3 = 5.333. The inverse distances are 5, 2.5, and 1.25, whose sum is 8.75. Dividing by that sum gives weights 4/7, 2/7, and 1/7. The weighted prediction is (4·3 + 2·5 + 1·8)/7 = 30/7, approximately 4.286.

Distance zero needs an explicit rule because division by zero is undefined. A common choice is to average the targets of exact matches and give the nonmatching points no weight. If several exact matches have conflicting targets, those observed targets still need to be combined. Weighting is a modeling choice: it may help or hurt, and validation should decide.

Weighted combinations also appear in attention, a mechanism used in transformer models. Learned query and key representations produce relevance scores, and normalized scores weight value vectors, often representing items in the available context. The common idea is to combine information with different influence. Transformer attention is not ordinary kNN over a training table and does not require a kd-tree; learned parameters and context-dependent values both participate. [7]

12. Keep the representation and the memory consistent

A complete retrieval-based predictor includes more than the final averaging or vote. The following order keeps the data roles and computation costs clear.

  1. Choose the representation and comparison. Decide what each feature means and what it should mean for two observations to be close.
  2. Fit or choose the transformation using the allowed data. Learn means and scales on training data. Save any learned feature map or sampled projection matrix.
  3. Transform and retain the training examples and targets. Build an index if the expected query workload and geometry justify it.
  4. Transform each new query with the same map. Retrieve candidates, combine their targets, and account for all query work.
  5. Evaluate choices on validation observations. Compare k, weights, representations, and search effort under the relevant metrics. Keep the test set for the final fixed procedure.

Changing the map can require transforming the catalog again and rebuilding its index. Changing only the query's requested k does not change the stored kd-tree. A system may combine a parametric representation, a non-parametric example memory, and a search index. Ask separately what was learned, what is retained, what is chosen, and what is computed when the next query arrives.

13. Check your understanding

  1. How can classic Shazam use exact token lookups while recognizing a noisy fragment that is not identical to a stored waveform?
  2. Why does cosine 1 not imply identical original vectors? What extra condition makes maximizing cosine equivalent to minimizing Euclidean distance?
  3. Eleven neighbors contain nine red labels and two blue labels. What are the uniform class prediction and red vote fraction? What would be unjustified about treating that fraction as a certainty?
  4. Explain zero training error for one-neighbor regression when rows can retrieve themselves. Why does the same argument not establish low validation error?
  5. Account for kd-tree construction by levels. How does replacing linear-time median selection with sorting every subset change the bound?
  6. For q = (5.95, 4.3), why can the region x₁ ≥ 6 not be pruned when the incumbent distance is 0.559? What does finding I at distance 0.25 change?
  7. A tree has logarithmic height and examines four points. Give two reasons that this does not establish a four-operation or logarithmic-time query.
  8. A build costs 0.6 ms, a full scan costs 0.04 ms per query, and an indexed query costs 0.01 ms. When is the index strictly cheaper? What if the indexed query costs 0.05 ms?
  9. Let U have shape 1,000 by 500 and R have shape 500 by 10. Give the shapes of U R and q R, the dense projection costs, and the reduced-space full-scan cost. Does the shape calculation guarantee the same nearest neighbors?
  10. Why does moving the fifth selected neighbor farther away leave a uniform five-neighbor mean unchanged? What changes with inverse-distance weights?
Reasoning for the practice questions
  1. The representation extracts robust tokens. Some tokens survive noise and match exactly; consistent offsets across many hits identify a recording. Exact token identity is different from raw-waveform identity.
  2. A positive multiple of a vector points in the same direction. For unit vectors, squared Euclidean distance is 2 minus twice their dot product, so the rankings agree.
  3. The prediction is red and the red fraction is 9/11. It is a local probability estimate; the neighborhood can be unrepresentative, the metric unsuitable, or the estimate poorly calibrated.
  4. A distinct training row has itself as a zero-distance neighbor, giving its own target. A fresh query has no such guarantee; noisy targets can mislead nearby predictions.
  5. With linear selection, each level processes n references in total and there are O(log n) levels, giving O(n log n) partition work. Repeated sorting adds decreasing logarithmic factors across those levels, totaling O(n log² n) for fixed dimension. Coordinates still require Θ(nd) storage.
  6. The region bound is only 0.05, below 0.559, so it may contain an improvement. Finding I shrinks the radius to 0.25, allowing any other region with lower bound greater than 0.25 to be pruned.
  7. A point distance itself costs Θ(d); region bounds, traversal, and candidate management add work. Backtracking can explore many branches, even in a balanced tree.
  8. The threshold is 0.6/(0.04 - 0.01) = 20 queries. Totals are equal at 20; the index is strictly cheaper from 21 queries onward. At 0.05 ms per indexed query, it starts with a build cost and is slower on every query, so this model has no break-even.
  9. U R is 1,000 by 10; q R is 1 by 10. Ordinary dense projection uses 5 million coordinate products for the catalog and 5,000 for a query. A reduced-space full scan uses 10,000 coordinate products. Top-k selection and any index work are additional. Shapes establish a valid multiplication, not a neighbor-preservation guarantee.
  10. Uniform averaging depends only on the five targets while the selected set stays fixed. Inverse-distance weighting changes the normalized contribution of the moved point and, through normalization, those of the other points.

Sources and further exploration

The interactive lecture contains the complete slide sequence. The companion notebook contains the classification, regression, audio, and search experiments. Numerical examples here distinguish measured experiment results, constructed arithmetic examples, and theoretical cost bounds.

  1. Avery Wang, An Industrial-Strength Audio Search Algorithm (2003). Classic fingerprint tokens and time-offset evidence.
  2. Sungkyun Chang and colleagues, Neural Audio Fingerprint for High-specific Audio Retrieval based on Contrastive Learning (2021). A separate learned-vector audio-retrieval system.
  3. Stanford NLP, GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation. Source of the course word vectors.
  4. scikit-learn, Nearest Neighbors and KDTree. Prediction rules, search methods, and query parameters.
  5. Russell A. Brown, Building a Balanced k-d Tree in O(kn log n) Time (2015). Construction variants; the paper uses k for coordinate dimension, which these notes call d.
  6. scikit-learn, Random Projection. Shared random maps and probabilistic distance-preservation guarantees.
  7. Ashish Vaswani and colleagues, Attention Is All You Need (2017). Relevance-weighted combinations in transformer attention.
